item.title: How much of the GPU did they actually use? R and Python in one post
item.dc:creator: Evan Pai
item.description:
My R post looked at what accelerators can do. My Python post looked at how much compute models used. This post joins the two to ask what every cluster engineer asks about a training run: what fraction of the hardware’s peak did it achieve?

That number, often called model FLOPs utilisation (MFU), can be estimated from public records:

The work is split between the two languages. R cleans the hardware specs, using the same approach as the R post. Python reads the model records, joins them and computes utilisation. R then plots the result. Objects cross between them through reticulate: Python reads R objects as r.name, and R reads Python objects as py$name.

Data. Two Epoch AI datasets, both licensed under CC BY 4.0: Data on Machine Learning Hardware and Data on AI Models (Epoch AI, published online at epoch.ai, accessed 23 Sep 2026). This post reuses the snapshots committed next to the two earlier posts, so no data is downloaded at build time.

Step 1 (R): clean the hardware table

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
library(reticulate)
hardware <- read_csv("../gpu-hardware-trends/ml_hardware.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(
    hardware = `Hardware name`,
    peak_flops = pmax(`Tensor-FP16/BF16 performance (FLOP/s)`,
                      `FP16 (half precision) performance (FLOP/s)`,
                      `FP32 (single precision) performance (FLOP/s)`, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(peak_flops), peak_flops > 0)

nrow(hardware)
[1] 162

This is a plain R data.frame. The next chunk is Python and reads it directly as r.hardware.

Step 2 (Python): join model records and compute utilisation

import sys
print(sys.executable)  # should be this project's .venv
/Users/evanpai/Desktop/UBC MDS/DSCI_521_computing_platform/DSCI_512_milestone2_evan1011/EvanPai.github.io/.venv/bin/python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

hardware = r.hardware  # the R data frame, now a pandas DataFrame
print(type(hardware).__name__, hardware.shape)
DataFrame (162, 2)
models = pd.read_csv("../ai-compute-scaling/notable_ai_models.csv")
runs = models.dropna(subset=["Training compute (FLOP)", "Training hardware",
                             "Hardware quantity", "Training time (hours)"]).copy()
runs["year"] = pd.to_datetime(runs["Publication date"]).dt.year
matched = runs.merge(hardware, left_on="Training hardware", right_on="hardware", how="inner")
print(f"{len(runs)} runs with compute, hardware, chip count and time; "
      f"{len(matched)} match a chip in the hardware table")
154 runs with compute, hardware, chip count and time; 140 match a chip in the hardware table

matched["utilisation"] = matched["Training compute (FLOP)"] / (
    matched["Hardware quantity"] * matched["peak_flops"] * matched["Training time (hours)"] * 3600
)
matched["plausible"] = matched["utilisation"].between(0.01, 1.0)

A circularity check before trusting the answer

A first plot of these numbers showed a suspicious pile-up just above 30%. Epoch’s Training compute notes column explains it. When a lab does not report compute, Epoch often estimates it from the hardware, as chips × peak × time × an assumed utilisation, usually 30–40%. For those rows, the formula above just returns Epoch’s assumption. It is circular.

So before measuring anything, I tag each run by how its compute was estimated. If the notes mention an assumed utilisation or an “estimate from hardware”, the run is tagged hardware-based. The others are independent: reported by the developer, or counted from parameters and tokens. Only the independent runs say anything about real utilisation. The tagging is a keyword heuristic, so it is approximate. The pattern is written out below so it can be checked.

assumed_pattern = (
    r"assum\w*[^.]{0,80}utili[sz]\w*"        # "30% utilization assumed", "assume 0.4 utilization"
    r"|utili[sz]\w*[^.]{0,40}assum\w*"
    r"|\d+\s*% (?:hardware )?utili[sz]\w*"   # "30% utilization"
    r"|0\.\d+ ?(?:hardware )?utili[sz]\w*"   # "0.3 utilization"
    r"|utili[sz]ation rate of"
    r"|hardware details|estimate from hardware"
)
notes = matched["Training compute notes"].fillna("")
matched["estimate"] = np.where(
    notes.str.contains(assumed_pattern, case=False, regex=True),
    "Hardware-based (utilisation assumed)",
    "Independent (reported or counted)",
)

utilisation = matched[["Model", "year", "hardware", "Hardware quantity", "utilisation",
                       "plausible", "estimate"]].rename(columns={"Hardware quantity": "chips"})
utilisation.groupby("estimate").agg(
    runs=("utilisation", "size"),
    flagged_implausible=("plausible", lambda p: int((~p).sum())),
)
                                      runs  flagged_implausible
estimate                                                       
Hardware-based (utilisation assumed)    76                    5
Independent (reported or counted)       64                   11

Runs outside 1–100% are flagged, not dropped. An estimate above 100% is physically impossible, so at least one input must be off. Common causes are a run trained in FP8 measured against a 16-bit peak, a chip count that includes idle spares, or a training time that leaves out restarts.

Step 3 (R): plot what Python computed

Back in R, py$utilisation is the pandas DataFrame from Step 2, converted to an R data.frame.

util <- py$utilisation

util |>
  filter(plausible) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, utilisation)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 0.28, ymax = 0.42,
           fill = "#e09f3e", alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_point(aes(size = chips), colour = "#1b6ca8", alpha = 0.6,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.25, height = 0, seed = 521)) +
  facet_wrap(~estimate, ncol = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 6, labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Publication year", y = "Estimated utilisation", size = "Chips") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
util |>
  filter(plausible) |>
  group_by(estimate) |>
  summarise(
    runs = n(),
    median = scales::percent(median(utilisation), accuracy = 1),
    `middle 50%` = paste(scales::percent(quantile(utilisation, c(0.25, 0.75)), accuracy = 1),
                         collapse = " to "),
    `inside the 28–42% band` = scales::percent(mean(between(utilisation, 0.28, 0.42)), accuracy = 1),
    `median chips` = median(chips)
  ) |>
  kable(caption = "Utilisation of plausible runs, by how the run's compute was estimated.")
Utilisation of plausible runs, by how the run’s compute was estimated.
estimate runs median middle 50% inside the 28–42% band median chips
Hardware-based (utilisation assumed) 71 30% 29% to 40% 65% 64
Independent (reported or counted) 53 30% 23% to 37% 45% 1024

What I found

  • Half the data would have answered with its own assumption. More than half of the runs that can be joined have compute estimated from the hardware, and most of them land inside the assumed 28–42% band. A naive analysis would have “discovered” that training runs achieve about 30% utilisation, which is exactly what was put in.
  • The independent runs are more informative, and they are wider. Their median is also close to 30%, so Epoch’s default is a reasonable prior. The spread is much larger, though. Real runs range from well under 20% to over 50%, and that spread is where a cluster team’s engineering work shows up.
  • Physical bounds are a cheap data check. Requiring 1–100% utilisation caught inconsistent records that a purely statistical filter would have kept.

How the languages split the work. R’s pmax(..., na.rm = TRUE) made the “best available precision” rule a one-liner. pandas handled the join, the regex tagging and the arithmetic. ggplot2 drew facets from a data frame created in Python. Nothing was written to disk between steps. The objects passed in memory through r.hardware and py$utilisation.

item.title: Predicting the compute behind an AI model, without leaking the answer
item.dc:creator: Evan Pai
item.description:
Labs rarely say how much compute a new model took. They do often say how many parameters it has, roughly how much data it saw, and who built it. This post asks two questions. How fast is training compute growing? And how well can it be estimated from the details that are public? The second one is a small but realistic ML problem. The labels are noisy, a third of the features are missing, two tempting columns leak the answer, and the model has to hold up on models released after the training data ends.

Data. Data on AI Models by Epoch AI (the Notable AI Models table), licensed under CC BY 4.0. Citation: Epoch AI, “Data on AI Models”. Published online at epoch.ai. Retrieved from https://epoch.ai/data/ai-models [online resource]. Accessed 23 Sep 2026. The table is updated daily, so I committed the snapshot downloaded on 23 September 2026 (notable_ai_models.csv, about 2.2 MB) next to this post. That keeps the numbers below reproducible.

Setup

import sys

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin, clone
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, RidgeCV
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, TimeSeriesSplit
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
rng = np.random.default_rng(521)

# Confirms the render used this project's uv environment, not a global Python.
print(sys.executable)
/Users/evanpai/Desktop/UBC MDS/DSCI_521_computing_platform/DSCI_512_milestone2_evan1011/EvanPai.github.io/.venv/bin/python3

Loading and cleaning

raw = pd.read_csv("notable_ai_models.csv")

models = raw.assign(
    date=pd.to_datetime(raw["Publication date"]),
    compute=raw["Training compute (FLOP)"],
    params=raw["Parameters"],
    # a handful of rows list several dataset sizes as "a,b"; those become NaN
    tokens=pd.to_numeric(raw["Training dataset size (total)"], errors="coerce"),
)
models["year"] = models["date"].dt.year + (models["date"].dt.dayofyear - 1) / 365.25

# Deep-learning era, and only rows where the target is known.
dl = models[(models["year"] >= 2010) & models["compute"].notna()].copy()
print(f"{len(raw)} notable models in total, {len(dl)} since 2010 with a compute estimate")
1072 notable models in total, 478 since 2010 with a compute estimate

Missing values are the main data problem, so I measure them before modelling anything.

cols = {
    "params": "Parameters",
    "tokens": "Training dataset size",
    "Training hardware": "Training hardware",
    "Open model weights?": "Open weights flag",
    "Training compute cost (2023 USD)": "Training cost",
}
(dl[list(cols)].isna().mean().rename(index=cols).to_frame("missing")
   .style.format("{:.0%}"))

How fast is training compute growing?

I regress log10(compute) on publication year. The slope is in orders of magnitude per year, so the doubling time is years. The data are uneven (many models from 2020 onwards, few from early years) and the residuals are far from normal. So instead of trusting the textbook standard error, I bootstrap: refit on 2,000 resampled datasets and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the doubling time.

def doubling_months(df):
    slope = np.polyfit(df["year"], np.log10(df["compute"]), 1)[0]
    return 12 * np.log10(2) / slope

def bootstrap(df, n=2000):
    idx = rng.integers(0, len(df), size=(n, len(df)))
    return np.array([doubling_months(df.iloc[i]) for i in idx])

subsets = {
    "All domains": dl,
    "Language": dl[dl["Domain"] == "Language"],
    "Vision": dl[dl["Domain"] == "Vision"],
}
rows = []
for name, df in subsets.items():
    boots = bootstrap(df)
    lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
    rows.append({"subset": name, "models": len(df),
                 "doubling time (months)": round(doubling_months(df), 1),
                 "95% bootstrap CI": f"{lo:.1f} to {hi:.1f}"})
pd.DataFrame(rows)
subset models doubling time (months) 95% bootstrap CI
0 All domains 478 5.7 5.4 to 6.1
1 Language 240 4.9 4.4 to 5.3
2 Vision 73 6.8 6.1 to 7.7 
domain_group = dl["Domain"].where(dl["Domain"].isin(["Language", "Vision", "Games"]), "Other / multimodal")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.6))
for (name, df), colour in zip(dl.groupby(domain_group), ["#e09f3e", "#d1495b", "#8a8a8a", "#1b6ca8"]):
    ax.scatter(df["year"], df["compute"], s=14, alpha=0.65, label=name, color=colour)
b, a = np.polyfit(dl["year"], np.log10(dl["compute"]), 1)
xs = np.linspace(dl["year"].min(), dl["year"].max(), 100)
ax.plot(xs, 10 ** (a + b * xs), color="black", lw=1.5)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("Publication year")
ax.set_ylabel("Training compute (FLOP)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")
plt.show()

Compute doubles roughly every six months. That is about three times faster than the hardware trend in my memory-wall post, where peak FLOP/s per chip doubles about every 1.6 years. Most of the growth therefore comes from using more chips for longer, not from faster chips.

Does C ≈ 6ND hold?

For dense transformers, training compute is often approximated as : parameters, training tokens, and 6 FLOPs per parameter per token (2 for the forward pass, 4 for the backward pass). If that holds, the two public numbers alone would almost pin down the answer. I check it on the language models that report all three quantities.

lang = dl[(dl["Domain"] == "Language") & dl["params"].notna() & dl["tokens"].notna()]
ratio = np.log10(lang["compute"] / (6 * lang["params"] * lang["tokens"]))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
ax.hist(ratio, bins=40, color="#1b6ca8", alpha=0.85)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("log10( reported compute / 6ND )")
ax.set_ylabel("models")
plt.show()

print(f"{len(lang)} language models; median ratio {10 ** ratio.median():.1f}x; "
      f"{(ratio.abs() <= np.log10(3)).mean():.0%} within a factor of 3, "
      f"{(ratio.abs() <= 1).mean():.0%} within a factor of 10")
200 language models; median ratio 3.2x; 32% within a factor of 3, 46% within a factor of 10

The typical language model reports about three times more compute than predicts, and only about half land within 10× of it. Several causes are known: training for more than one epoch, dataset sizes reported in words or documents rather than tokens, mixture-of-experts models where only a fraction of is active per token, and plain uncertainty in the estimates. is a useful feature, not a substitute for the label.

A leakage-aware model of training compute

Task. Predict log10(compute) from information that is public when a model is announced: parameters, dataset size, the estimate, publication year, domain, organisation type, country and whether weights are open. The error is measured in orders of magnitude, so an MAE of 1.0 means a typical miss of 10×.

Leakage. Two columns look useful and must be dropped. Frontier model is defined by Epoch as being among the top models by training compute. Training compute cost is computed from training compute. Either one would give a great test score and a useless model.

Validation. The split is by time. The model trains on everything published before 2023 and is tested on 2023 onwards. A random split would let it learn from 2025 models when predicting 2022 ones, and deployment never offers that luxury. Hyperparameters are tuned with TimeSeriesSplit inside the training period only.

def build_features(df):
    X = pd.DataFrame(index=df.index)
    X["log_params"] = np.log10(df["params"])
    X["log_tokens"] = np.log10(df["tokens"])
    X["log_6nd"] = np.log10(6 * df["params"] * df["tokens"])
    X["year"] = df["year"]
    X["domain"] = df["Domain"].str.split(",").str[0]
    X["org_type"] = df["Organization categorization"].str.split(",").str[0].fillna("Unknown")
    X["country"] = df["Country (of organization)"].str.split(",").str[0].fillna("Unknown")
    X["open_weights"] = df["Open model weights?"].fillna("Unknown")
    return X

numeric = ["log_params", "log_tokens", "log_6nd", "year"]
categorical = ["domain", "org_type", "country", "open_weights"]

dl = dl.sort_values("date")
X, y = build_features(dl), np.log10(dl["compute"])
train, test = dl["year"] < 2023, dl["year"] >= 2023
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = X[train], X[test], y[train], y[test]
print(f"train: {train.sum()} models (2010-2022)   test: {test.sum()} models (2023 onwards)")
train: 306 models (2010-2022)   test: 172 models (2023 onwards)

Why trees need help here. Gradient-boosted trees predict with piecewise constants, so they cannot extrapolate. For any year after 2022 they answer as if it were 2022. The target, however, grows by roughly two orders of magnitude a year. The fix is to detrend. A linear regression on year captures the trend, and the trees model only what is left. Detrended below wraps any scikit-learn regressor this way, so it can be tuned with GridSearchCV like any other.

class Detrended(BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin):
    """Fit a linear trend on `year`, then fit `estimator` to the residuals."""

    def __init__(self, estimator):
        self.estimator = estimator

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.trend_ = LinearRegression().fit(X[["year"]], y)
        self.estimator_ = clone(self.estimator).fit(X, y - self.trend_.predict(X[["year"]]))
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.trend_.predict(X[["year"]]) + self.estimator_.predict(X)

I compare five models. Two are baselines: the training median, and a trend-only regression on year. Ridge regression uses median imputation, missingness indicators and one-hot categories. Gradient boosting is fitted once on the raw target and once detrended. Boosting handles missing values natively and is tuned with time-series cross-validation.

linear_prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True), StandardScaler()), numeric),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", min_frequency=5), categorical),
])
tree_prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", "passthrough", numeric),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", min_frequency=5, sparse_output=False), categorical),
])

def gbm():
    return make_pipeline(tree_prep, HistGradientBoostingRegressor(loss="absolute_error", random_state=0))

grid = {
    "histgradientboostingregressor__max_depth": [2, 3, None],
    "histgradientboostingregressor__learning_rate": [0.03, 0.1],
    "histgradientboostingregressor__max_iter": [200, 400],
}
cv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)
search_raw = GridSearchCV(gbm(), grid, cv=cv, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").fit(X_train, y_train)
search_detrended = GridSearchCV(
    Detrended(gbm()), {f"estimator__{k}": v for k, v in grid.items()},
    cv=cv, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error",
).fit(X_train, y_train)

fitted = {
    "Median baseline": DummyRegressor(strategy="median").fit(X_train, y_train),
    "Trend-only baseline": Detrended(DummyRegressor(strategy="constant", constant=0)).fit(X_train, y_train),
    "Ridge regression": make_pipeline(linear_prep, RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-2, 3, 20))).fit(X_train, y_train),
    "Gradient boosting, raw target": search_raw.best_estimator_,
    "Gradient boosting, detrended": search_detrended.best_estimator_,
}
print("detrended boosting, best params:",
      {k.split("__")[-1]: v for k, v in search_detrended.best_params_.items()})
detrended boosting, best params: {'learning_rate': 0.03, 'max_depth': None, 'max_iter': 400}

The test set mixes two very different populations. Most models report their parameter count. A minority do not, and those are mostly large closed models. So the scores are split by that.

known = X_test["log_params"].notna()

def score(name, model):
    err = np.abs(y_test - model.predict(X_test))
    return {"model": name,
            "MAE, all": round(err.mean(), 2),
            f"MAE, params known (n={known.sum()})": round(err[known].mean(), 2),
            f"MAE, params missing (n={(~known).sum()})": round(err[~known].mean(), 2),
            "within 10x": f"{(err <= 1).mean():.0%}"}

pd.DataFrame([score(name, m) for name, m in fitted.items()])

Both baselines matter. The median is useless because compute keeps growing, and the trend on its own does much better. Raw boosting comes out worse than ridge regression because it cannot extrapolate. Detrending fixes that. It gives the best overall score and the smallest error on the hard rows, and it ties ridge where parameters are known. The gap between the two MAE columns is the main result. When the parameter count is public, a typical miss is well under an order of magnitude. When it is hidden, the model misses by two or more.

For comparison, on the test rows where it can be computed, the rule on its own:

best = fitted["Gradient boosting, detrended"]
has_6nd = X_test["log_6nd"].notna()
err_6nd = np.abs(y_test[has_6nd] - X_test.loc[has_6nd, "log_6nd"])
err_best = np.abs(y_test[has_6nd] - best.predict(X_test[has_6nd]))
pd.DataFrame({"MAE (log10)": [err_6nd.mean(), err_best.mean()],
              "within 10x": [(err_6nd <= 1).mean(), (err_best <= 1).mean()]},
             index=[f"6ND rule (n={has_6nd.sum()})", "Detrended boosting, same rows"]).round(2)
MAE (log10) within 10x
6ND rule (n=103) 1.08 0.53
Detrended boosting, same rows 0.74 0.79

What the model relies on

Permutation importance on the test set measures how much the error grows when one feature is shuffled. That shows what the model needs on data it has not seen, which the impurity scores computed during training cannot show.

imp = permutation_importance(best, X_test, y_test, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error",
                             n_repeats=30, random_state=0)
order = np.argsort(imp.importances_mean)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
ax.barh(np.array(X_test.columns)[order], imp.importances_mean[order],
        xerr=imp.importances_std[order], color="#1b6ca8", alpha=0.85)
ax.set_xlabel("Increase in test MAE (log10 FLOP)")
plt.show()

Parameters and year carry almost all of the signal. The surprise is that log_tokens and log_6nd have negative importance. Shuffling them makes the test error smaller. The model learned how dataset size related to compute before 2023, and that relationship changed afterwards. Recent models are routinely trained on far more tokens per parameter than their predecessors, and the data-size field mixes tokens, words and images across domains. That is a concrete case of distribution shift, and it can be tested directly: refit the same pipeline without the two features and see whether the test error drops.

data_features = ["log_tokens", "log_6nd"]
ablated = GridSearchCV(
    Detrended(make_pipeline(
        ColumnTransformer([
            ("num", "passthrough", [c for c in numeric if c not in data_features]),
            ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", min_frequency=5, sparse_output=False), categorical),
        ]),
        HistGradientBoostingRegressor(loss="absolute_error", random_state=0),
    )),
    {f"estimator__{k}": v for k, v in grid.items()},
    cv=cv, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error",
).fit(X_train, y_train)

pd.DataFrame([
    {"features": "all", "CV MAE (train period)": -search_detrended.best_score_,
     "test MAE": np.abs(y_test - best.predict(X_test)).mean()},
    {"features": "without dataset size and 6ND", "CV MAE (train period)": -ablated.best_score_,
     "test MAE": np.abs(y_test - ablated.predict(X_test)).mean()},
]).round(2)
features CV MAE (train period) test MAE
0 all 1.07 1.03
1 without dataset size and 6ND 1.12 0.92

The two scores disagree, and that disagreement is the signature of the shift. Inside the training period, the dataset-size features help (CV MAE 1.07 vs 1.12). On 2023+ models they hurt (test MAE 1.03 vs 0.92).

This table is the honest version of feature selection. Cross-validation inside the training period is the only score that can pick features, because choosing by test score would leak the test set into the model. Test MAE is shown here to diagnose the shift, not to make the choice. I keep the full model as the main result, because it is the one the training-period evidence supports.

Where it fails

Aggregate scores hide the cases that matter. Below, test error is broken down by Epoch’s own confidence rating for each compute estimate, followed by the largest individual misses.

test_df = dl[test].assign(pred=best.predict(X_test), err=lambda d: np.log10(d["compute"]) - d["pred"])
by_conf = (test_df.groupby("Confidence")["err"]
           .agg(models="size", MAE=lambda e: e.abs().mean().round(2))
           .reindex(["Confident", "Likely", "Speculative"]))
display(by_conf)

worst = (test_df.assign(abs_err=test_df["err"].abs())
         .nlargest(6, "abs_err")
         [["Model", "Organization", "params", "compute", "pred", "err"]]
         .assign(compute=lambda d: d["compute"].map("{:.1e}".format),
                 pred=lambda d: (10 ** d["pred"]).map("{:.1e}".format),
                 params=lambda d: d["params"].map(lambda p: "not disclosed" if pd.isna(p) else f"{p:.1e}"),
                 err=lambda d: d["err"].round(2))
         .rename(columns={"compute": "actual FLOP", "pred": "predicted FLOP",
                          "err": "error (log10)"}))
worst
models MAE
Confidence
Confident 100 0.80
Likely 51 1.12
Speculative 21 1.91
Model Organization params actual FLOP predicted FLOP error (log10)
342 PeptideBERT Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) not disclosed 4.9e+16 1.6e+21 -4.51
172 GPT-4.5 OpenAI not disclosed 3.8e+26 3.9e+22 3.99
295 Gemini 1.0 Ultra Google DeepMind not disclosed 5.0e+25 8.1e+21 3.79
340 Swift Intel Labs 5.7e+04 5.3e+16 2.9e+20 -3.73
346 AudioLM Google Research 1.5e+09 3.9e+18 1.7e+22 -3.65
8 GPT-6 Astra OpenAI not disclosed 1.0e+27 3.0e+23 3.52

Errors grow steadily from “Confident” to “Speculative” labels. Part of what looks like model error is noise in the target itself.

The largest misses fail in two opposite directions, and both come from the same cause. The year trend is a strong prior, and the model falls back on it when the size information is weak or missing.

  • Under-prediction of flagship closed models (GPT-4.5, Gemini 1.0 Ultra and others). Their parameter count is not disclosed. This is missing not at random: labs withhold size most often for their largest models, so median imputation plus a missingness flag cannot recover information that was hidden because it was large.
  • Over-prediction of small specialised models (a peptide model, a 57-thousand-parameter drone-racing controller, an audio model). Being published after 2023 pulls the prediction toward the frontier, even when the model is tiny.

Doing better would take signals from outside this table, such as API pricing, context length or benchmark scores for closed models, rather than a fancier algorithm.

What I found

  • Training compute for notable models doubles about every 6 months, and for language models about every 5. The bootstrap intervals are tight. Per-chip hardware in my memory-wall post doubles about every 19 months, so most of the growth comes from larger clusters and longer runs, not faster chips.
  • is a rough guide, not a law. The typical language model reports about 3× more compute than it predicts, and only about half land within 10×.
  • Model choice has to match the extrapolation problem. With a time-based split, raw gradient boosting loses to ridge regression because trees cannot extrapolate. Detrending turns it into the best model.
  • The data-size features drifted. They help in cross-validation before 2023 and hurt afterwards. Permutation importance on held-out data caught this, and an ablation confirmed it.
  • Missing data is the real ceiling. When the parameter count is public, the typical miss is well under 10×, and on rows where exists the model beats the rule alone (MAE 0.74 vs 1.08). For flagship closed models it does not, and the reason is why the data is missing, not the choice of algorithm.

Caveats. The “notable” filter is Epoch’s editorial choice, so this is not a random sample of all models. Many compute labels are themselves estimates, some built from , which flatters the physics features. Speculative labels are the hardest to predict. Weighting training rows by label confidence is a natural next step.

item.title: The memory wall, measured: 18 years of ML accelerators
item.dc:creator: Evan Pai
item.description:
Every GPU launch comes with a headline FLOP/s number, and every generation that number jumps. When I was tuning LLM inference on H100s, though, the question that kept coming up was how fast weights could be pulled out of memory, not how fast they could be multiplied. This post checks that intuition against data: across every ML accelerator Epoch AI has catalogued, how fast has peak compute grown, how fast has memory bandwidth grown, and how wide is the gap now?

Data. Data on Machine Learning Hardware by Epoch AI, licensed under CC BY 4.0. Citation: Epoch AI, “Data on Machine Learning Hardware”. Published online at epoch.ai. Retrieved from https://epoch.ai/data/machine-learning-hardware [online resource]. Accessed 23 Sep 2026. The dataset is updated continuously, so I committed the snapshot downloaded on 23 September 2026 (ml_hardware.csv, about 100 KB) next to this post. That way the numbers below do not change between builds.

Loading the data

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
hardware_raw <- read_csv("ml_hardware.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(hardware_raw)
[1] 176  39

Each row is one chip: 176 accelerators, with 39 columns of specs. Most of those columns are sparsely filled. Vendors publish different numbers, and precision formats change between generations. So the first job is to decide which columns to trust and what to do when one is missing.

Cleaning: one comparable “peak compute” number per chip

Chips before 2017 have no tensor cores, and many recent chips only publish tensor-core numbers. I keep three columns: tensor FP16/BF16, plain FP16 and FP32. The headline “peak” is the largest of the three. Taking the largest rather than preferring 16-bit matters. Consumer Pascal cards from 2016 run FP16 at 1/64 of their FP32 rate, so preferring 16-bit would record those chips as roughly 60× slower than they really are. The precision column records which format supplied the peak, so the mix stays visible.

hardware <- hardware_raw |>
  transmute(
    name         = `Hardware name`,
    manufacturer = Manufacturer,
    type         = Type,
    release      = as.Date(`Release date`),
    tensor16     = `Tensor-FP16/BF16 performance (FLOP/s)`,
    fp16         = `FP16 (half precision) performance (FLOP/s)`,
    fp32         = `FP32 (single precision) performance (FLOP/s)`,
    bandwidth    = `Memory bandwidth (byte/s)`,
    memory       = `Memory (bytes)`,
    price        = `Release price (USD)`
  ) |>
  mutate(
    peak = pmax(tensor16, fp16, fp32, na.rm = TRUE),
    precision = case_when(
      peak == tensor16 ~ "Tensor FP16/BF16",
      peak == fp16     ~ "FP16",
      peak == fp32     ~ "FP32",
      .default         = NA_character_
    ),
    year = as.numeric(format(release, "%Y")) +
      (as.numeric(format(release, "%j")) - 1) / 365.25
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(release), peak > 0 | bandwidth > 0)

hardware |>
  summarise(
    chips = n(),
    first_release = min(release),
    last_release = max(release),
    with_peak = sum(!is.na(peak) & peak > 0),
    with_bandwidth = sum(!is.na(bandwidth)),
    with_both = sum(!is.na(peak) & peak > 0 & !is.na(bandwidth))
  ) |>
  kable(caption = "Coverage of the cleaned hardware table.")
Coverage of the cleaned hardware table.
chips first_release last_release with_peak with_bandwidth with_both
160 2008-06-16 2026-03-11 155 149 144

Compute and bandwidth over time

trend_data <- hardware |>
  select(name, year, `Peak compute (FLOP/s)` = peak,
         `Memory bandwidth (byte/s)` = bandwidth) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(name, year), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value), value > 0)

ggplot(trend_data, aes(year, value, colour = metric)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_log()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1b6ca8", "#d1495b")) +
  labs(x = "Release year", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

The two clouds in Figure 1 start about three orders of magnitude apart and drift further apart every year. The slopes can be turned into a number that is easier to reason about: the doubling time. If log2(value) = a + b * year, then the value doubles every 1 / b years. I fit one regression per metric and turn the 95% confidence interval on b into an interval on the doubling time.

doubling <- function(df, column) {
  d <- df |> filter(!is.na(.data[[column]]), .data[[column]] > 0)
  fit <- lm(log2(d[[column]]) ~ d$year)
  slope <- coef(fit)[2]
  ci <- confint(fit)[2, ]
  tibble(
    n = nrow(d),
    `growth per year` = sprintf("%.2fx", 2^slope),
    `doubling time (years)` = sprintf("%.2f", 1 / slope),
    `95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", 1 / ci[2], 1 / ci[1])
  )
}

doubling_table <- bind_rows(
  `Peak compute, any format`          = doubling(hardware, "peak"),
  `FP32 compute only`                 = doubling(hardware, "fp32"),
  `Memory bandwidth`                  = doubling(hardware, "bandwidth"),
  `Memory capacity`                   = doubling(hardware, "memory"),
  .id = "metric"
)
kable(doubling_table, caption = "Doubling times from log-linear fits over all chips with a release date.")
Doubling times from log-linear fits over all chips with a release date.
metric n growth per year doubling time (years) 95% CI
Peak compute, any format 155 1.55x 1.58 1.44 to 1.76
FP32 compute only 126 1.28x 2.77 2.45 to 3.18
Memory bandwidth 149 1.28x 2.84 2.42 to 3.43
Memory capacity 133 1.26x 2.99 2.45 to 3.83

Peak compute doubles about every year and a half. Memory bandwidth and capacity take close to three years. The FP32-only row was meant as a robustness check, and it changed my reading of the result. FP32 compute has grown at almost exactly the same rate as bandwidth. The confidence intervals overlap almost completely. On the chips’ traditional arithmetic path, the memory wall does not exist in this data. The entire gap comes from the tensor cores and lower-precision formats that vendors added from 2017 onward. So the memory wall is not a law of silicon. It is a consequence of the industry spending its transistor budget on dense low-precision matrix units.

What the gap means: the roofline ridge point

The roofline model gives this gap a concrete meaning. A kernel with arithmetic intensity (FLOPs performed per byte moved from memory) can run at most at . The crossover is the ridge point. Kernels below it are memory-bound and kernels above it are compute-bound. If compute grows faster than bandwidth, the ridge point moves right, and more real workloads end up memory-bound. Figure 2 and the table below show exactly that happening, in step with the spread of tensor cores.

flagships <- c(
  "NVIDIA Tesla V100 SXM2 16 GB", "NVIDIA A100 SXM4 80 GB",
  "NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80GB", "NVIDIA B200", "NVIDIA GB300 (Blackwell Ultra)",
  "AMD Instinct MI300X", "AMD Instinct MI355X",
  "Google TPU v3", "Google TPU v4", "Google TPU v7 Ironwood"
)

ridge <- hardware |>
  filter(!is.na(peak), peak > 0, !is.na(bandwidth)) |>
  mutate(ridge = peak / bandwidth, flagship = name %in% flagships)
labelled <- c("NVIDIA Tesla V100 SXM2 16 GB", "NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80GB",
              "NVIDIA GB300 (Blackwell Ultra)")

ggplot(ridge, aes(year, ridge)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = precision), alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  geom_text(
    data = filter(ridge, name %in% labelled),
    aes(label = sub(" \\(.*\\)", "", sub("NVIDIA (Tesla )?", "", name))),
    size = 3, vjust = -1, hjust = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#8a8a8a", "#e09f3e", "#1b6ca8")) +
  labs(x = "Release year", y = "FLOPs per byte (log scale)", colour = "Peak measured as") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
ridge |>
  mutate(era = cut(year, c(2008, 2016, 2020, 2023, 2027), right = FALSE,
                   labels = c("2008–2015", "2016–2019", "2020–2022", "2023–2026"))) |>
  group_by(era) |>
  summarise(
    chips = n(),
    `median ridge (FLOP/byte)` = round(median(ridge)),
    `share with tensor-core peak` = percent(mean(precision == "Tensor FP16/BF16"))
  ) |>
  kable(caption = "Median ridge point by release era.")
Median ridge point by release era.
era chips median ridge (FLOP/byte) share with tensor-core peak
2008–2015 17 17 0%
2016–2019 41 115 32%
2020–2022 43 184 47%
2023–2026 43 218 74%

Consequence for LLM inference

The ridge point explains something every LLM serving engineer runs into. When you generate one token at batch size 1, every weight is read once and used for about two FLOPs (one multiply, one add). With 16-bit weights that is 2 bytes per parameter, so the arithmetic intensity is roughly 1 FLOP per byte. The flagships above have ridge points in the hundreds. Single-stream decoding therefore uses well under 1% of the chip’s peak compute, and memory bandwidth sets the speed limit:

params <- 70e9  # a 70B-parameter model in 16-bit weights

ridge |>
  filter(flagship) |>
  arrange(release) |>
  transmute(
    chip = name,
    released = format(release, "%Y-%m"),
    `peak (TFLOP/s)` = round(peak / 1e12),
    `bandwidth (TB/s)` = round(bandwidth / 1e12, 2),
    `ridge (FLOP/byte)` = round(ridge),
    `70B decode ceiling (tok/s, batch 1)` = round(bandwidth / (2 * params), 1),
    `peak compute used at batch 1` = percent(1 / ridge, accuracy = 0.01)
  ) |>
  kable(caption = "Bandwidth-bound decode ceiling for a 70B model on one chip, ignoring KV-cache traffic and assuming the weights fit.")
Bandwidth-bound decode ceiling for a 70B model on one chip, ignoring KV-cache traffic and assuming the weights fit.
chip released peak (TFLOP/s) bandwidth (TB/s) ridge (FLOP/byte) 70B decode ceiling (tok/s, batch 1) peak compute used at batch 1
NVIDIA Tesla V100 SXM2 16 GB 2017-06 125 0.90 139 6.4 0.72%
Google TPU v3 2018-05 123 0.90 137 6.4 0.73%
NVIDIA A100 SXM4 80 GB 2020-11 312 2.04 153 14.6 0.65%
Google TPU v4 2021-05 275 1.20 229 8.6 0.44%
NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80GB 2022-09 989 3.35 295 23.9 0.34%
AMD Instinct MI300X 2023-12 1307 5.30 247 37.9 0.41%
NVIDIA B200 2024-11 2250 7.70 292 55.0 0.34%
AMD Instinct MI355X 2025-06 2517 8.00 315 57.1 0.32%
NVIDIA GB300 (Blackwell Ultra) 2025-08 2500 8.00 312 57.1 0.32%
Google TPU v7 Ironwood 2025-11 2307 7.37 313 52.6 0.32%

This is why serving systems like vLLM work so hard on batching. With a batch of sequences, each weight read from memory is used times, so arithmetic intensity grows roughly linearly in . The batch can climb toward the ridge point before compute becomes the limit. Continuous batching was one of the main levers when I tuned a LLaMA 3.1 70B chatbot on H100s for throughput, and this table shows why.

What I found

  • Across 18 years of accelerators, peak compute doubled every ~1.6 years against ~2.8 years for memory bandwidth.
  • The gap comes from tensor cores. FP32 compute kept pace with bandwidth. The divergence is the low-precision matrix hardware added since 2017.
  • The median ridge point rose from 17 to over 200 FLOPs per byte, more than an order of magnitude. A kernel now needs far more reuse of each byte before it can use the chip it runs on.
  • For LLM decoding at small batch sizes, that makes bandwidth, not FLOP/s, the number to read on a spec sheet, and batching, KV-cache layout and quantisation the levers that matter.

Caveats. These are vendor peak specs, not measured throughput. Each chip counts once however widely it was deployed. The log-linear fit treats a consumer card and a TPU pod chip as the same kind of point. A deployment-weighted analysis would be a natural next step.

item.title: My first weeks in MDS
item.dc:creator: Evan Pai
item.description:
Orientation week was mostly logistics — accounts, laptops, a room full of people introducing themselves — but the part that stuck with me was how quickly the cohort stopped being strangers. Everyone had arrived from somewhere different: economics, biology, public health, a few people coming back after years of work. I had half expected a room of computer science graduates like me, and instead spent the week being reminded that most of the interesting questions in this field arrive from somewhere other than the code.

Then classes started, and the pace was the real surprise. I knew MDS was compressed; I had not internalised what a block schedule feels like from the inside. A topic is introduced, you use it in a lab two days later, and by the following week it is assumed knowledge. Coming from a background where I would spend a week profiling a single application before changing anything, the instinct to understand a thing completely before starting stopped working almost immediately. What replaced it was starting before I felt ready and letting the gaps show up in the error messages.

A few weeks in, I have settled somewhere between overwhelmed and genuinely enjoying it. The tooling has been the easiest part to love — Git and the shell I already knew from cluster work, and Quarto has quietly replaced a pile of habits I did not realise were slowing me down; this site is a direct result. The statistics is where I am working hardest, and that is exactly why I came. I spent my undergraduate years making models run faster without being able to say much about whether their results deserved the compute. That is the gap I am here to close. Ask me again after the first round of quizzes.
